messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Kofi's Story

Kofi was fifty-five when his younger brother Emmanuel collapsed on a Sunday afternoon in their shared workshop. Emmanuel had been mixing paint, the same way he had done a hundred times before, when he simply fell. Kofi found him on the concrete floor, already unresponsive, and the next hours dissolved into a chaos of sirens, fluorescent hospital lights, and the terrible knowledge that Emmanuel was gone before the ambulance even arrived. A massive stroke, the doctors said. No warning. No chance. For three weeks Kofi had moved through the funeral arrangements in a state of numb compliance, but the moment he tried to return to work—to the very workshop where it happened—everything fractured.

Now, eight months later, the sound of an ambulance siren sends Kofi's entire body rigid. His chest tightens, his hands clench into fists, and a surge of dread floods through him that has nothing to do with the present moment and everything to do with that Sunday. The siren pulls up memories he cannot quite see but can feel with overwhelming force—the smell of the workshop, the weight of Emmanuel's limp arm, the specific timbre of the paramedic's voice calling out vitals. These fragments arrive not as coherent images but as raw emotional intensity, a drowning sensation that leaves him gasping. When conversations turn to loss—a colleague mentioning his mother's passing, a news story about someone who died unexpectedly—Kofi finds himself transported back to the workshop floor, his body flooding with the same grief and helplessness he felt holding his brother's hand in the hospital. The trigger itself resurrects the memory, and the memory resurrects the terror.

What troubles Kofi most is how these intrusions have reshaped his understanding of himself and his world. He has come to believe that his life has been destroyed, that the man he was before that Sunday—the steady craftsman, the reliable older brother, the man his wife depended on—no longer exists. This conviction feeds a constant vigilance that exhausts him. At night, he lies awake beside his wife, his body tense and primed for catastrophe, convinced that something else is about to be taken from him. He feels on guard even inside his own home, where he should feel safe. The darkness seems to amplify his sense of isolation; he feels set apart from others who have not experienced this sudden, senseless loss. When he looks at his wife, he sees someone he might lose at any moment, and this thought—this certainty that disaster is imminent—keeps his nervous system locked in a state of perpetual readiness. His shoulders ache from the tension. He grinds his teeth at night.

The workshop itself has become impossible. Kofi tried to return three months after the funeral, thinking routine would help, but the moment he stepped through the door, his body flooded with the memory of Emmanuel on the floor. The visual images came then—Emmanuel's face, the way his body had looked, the exact angle of his arm—and with them came a wave of overwhelming grief so profound it stopped his breath. Because of these memories, because they are so vivid and so devastating, Kofi has come to believe that returning to work means accepting that Emmanuel is truly gone, that the workshop is now a place of death rather than creation. This belief has deepened his sense that his identity as a painter, as a craftsman, has been erased. He has not worked in five months. His wife has taken on more hours at her job; tension between them has grown quiet and strained.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was an ambulance that passed his house last week. The siren triggered such an intense wave of dread and grief—the full emotional weight of the trauma without any clear image, just pure anguish—that he found himself unable to move for two hours afterward. He sat in his living room, body trembling, convinced that his wife would be next, that he was cursed to lose everyone he loved. When she came home and found him like that, she insisted he talk to someone. Kofi agreed, though part of him wonders if anyone can help him understand why his brother was taken, or how he is supposed to live in a world where such arbitrary loss is possible.
